Risk Management Plan (RMP) Executive Summary

Facility Name: Town of White Lake 
Address: 1879 White Lake Drive, PMB 7250, White Lake, NC 28337
Date: 09/02/2025

1. Accidental Release Prevention and Emergency Response Policies

At the Town of White Lake, we are committed to ensuring the safe storage, handling, and use of chlorine gas in our water treatment operations. We adhere strictly to all applicable EPA and OSHA regulations regarding hazardous substances. Our prevention program includes employee training, process safety information, mechanical integrity checks, and regular hazard analysis. In the unlikely event of an accidental chlorine release, our trained emergency response team will implement our site-specific emergency response plan in coordination with local emergency services to minimize impacts to workers, the community, and the environment.

2. Facility and Regulated Substances Handled

This facility uses chlorine gas as part of its water chlorination process. Chlorine is delivered and stored on-site in one-ton (2,000 lb) containers. The maximum intended inventory at any one time is typically two(2) ton containers, or approximately 4000 lbs of chlorine gas.

Chlorine is classified as a regulated toxic substance under EPAs Risk Management Program, with a threshold quantity of 2,500 lbs. Our maximum inventory exceeds this threshold, making this facility subject to RMP regulations.

3. Offsite Consequence Analysis

As part of the RMP, we conducted an Offsite Consequence Analysis (OCA) for a worst-case and alternative release scenario:

Worst-Case Scenario: Assumes the complete release of a full 2,000 lb ton container of liquified chlorine gas over 10 minutes due to container failure. Based on EPA modeling assumptions (e.g., urban topography, Class F stability, and 1.5 m/s wind speed), this scenario could affect receptors (e.g., public areas, residences, or environmental receptors) within a distance of approximately 3-miles.

Alternative Scenario: Represen

ts a more realistic release scenario, such as a transfer hose, a valve, or gasket failure leading to a smaller, slower leak. The release rate and impact radius are significantly reduced compared to the worst-case. This scenario may result in a chlorine plume affecting areas within .3 miles, depending on meteorological and topographic factors.

Both analyses were conducted using EPAs RMP*Comp or equivalent modeling software.

4. General Accidental Release Prevention Program

The Town of White Lake complies with OSHA's Process Safety Management (PSM) standard and EPA's Risk Management Program requirements. Key elements of our prevention program include:

Process hazard analyses (PHAs) updated every 5 years

Standard operating procedures (SOPs) for chlorine handling

Routine inspections and maintenance of chlorine containers and feed systems

Employee training in chlorine safety and emergency response

Safety instrumentation, gas detection, and automatic shut-off systems

Preventive maintenance and mechanical integrity program

5. Five-Year Accident History

In the past five years, The Town of White Lake has zero accidental releases of chlorine that resulted in on-site or off-site impacts:

6. Emergency Response Program

Our facility has a comprehensive Emergency Response Program in place. This includes:

Coordination with the Local Emergency Planning Committee (LEPC)

Facility-specific Emergency Response Plan (ERP)

Periodic drills and coordination with Bladen County Emergency Management, the local fire department, and hazmat responders

We maintain communication with local authorities to ensure that our plan aligns with community emergency procedures.

7. Planned Changes to Improve Safety

We are committed to continuous improvement and have identified the following safety enhancements:

Additional operator training in advanced chlorine leak response

Evaluation of alternative, safer disinfection technologies where feasible
